tip: 'Sebelum' (before) takes a verb directly: 'sebelum tidur' = before sleeping.
'Sambil' = while (one person, two actions): 'makan sambil membaca' = eat while reading.
'Pulang' packs 'go home' into one word – 'langsung pulang' = head straight home. There is no separate word for 'home' in the sentence.
'-kan' makes a verb act on someone: 'bangun' (wake up) → 'membangunkan' (wake someone up).
'-kan' can mean doing it for someone: 'membaca' (read) → 'membacakan' (read aloud to someone).
'Sarapan' is a verb all by itself – 'Saya sarapan roti' is literally 'I breakfast bread'. No word for 'have' or 'eat' needed.
When ordering, the number usually follows the dish: 'nasi goreng satu' – literally 'fried rice, one'.
'Sekali' means very but comes after the adjective: 'enak sekali' = very tasty, literally 'tasty very'.
'Boleh minta ...?' politely asks for something: 'Boleh minta air?' = May I have water?
'-nya' can mean the/its: 'rasa' (taste) → 'rasanya' (the taste of it).
'Kami' means we/our but excludes the person you're talking to: 'pesanan kami' = our order, not yours. 'Kita' would include them.
'Silakan' politely invites someone to act: 'silakan makan' = please eat.
'Yang' turns a description into 'the one that': 'yang lebih besar' = the bigger one.
'Itu' comes after its noun: 'toko itu' = that shop, literally 'shop that'. 'Ini' (this) follows its noun the same way.
'Di-' makes a verb passive: 'tawar' (bargain) → 'ditawar' (be bargained over).
'Dulu' after a verb means first: 'coba dulu' = try it first.
'Belum' means not yet: 'Pesanan saya belum datang'. Use 'belum', not 'tidak', for anything that could still happen.
'Lebih ... daripada' compares: 'lebih murah daripada di hotel' = cheaper than at the hotel.
Indonesian sorts siblings by age, not gender: 'kakak' = older sibling, 'adik' = younger. 'Dua kakak' never tells you brother or sister.
The possessor comes after the noun: 'ibu saya' = my mother, literally 'mother I'.
Adjectives follow their noun: 'kopi hitam' is literally 'coffee black'. Noun first, adjective second – the reverse of English.
'Kami' = we (not you); 'kita' = we (with you): 'keluarga kami' = our family.
'-nya' on a noun = his/her: 'ibunya' = his/her mother.
No word for 'is' before adjectives: 'Rumahnya besar' = His house (is) big.
'Sudah ... belum?' = already or not yet: 'Sudah makan belum?' = Eaten yet?
'Itu' (that) comes after its noun: 'anak laki-laki itu' = literally 'child male that'. 'Ini' (this) works the same way.
Comparisons borrow 'dari' (from) for 'than': 'lebih muda dari ayah saya' = literally 'more young from my father'.
Verbs never change for past time: 'menikah' stays the same. 'Tahun lalu' (last year) alone signals it already happened.
Doubling a noun usually makes it plural: 'anak-anak' = children.
'Berapa' (how much) asks age: 'Berapa umur kamu' = literally 'how-much age you'. No verb, no word order flip.
